questions.question: What are semantic HTML elements, and why do they matter?
questions.title: Semantic HTML meaning and benefits
questions.direct_answer: Semantic HTML elements describe the meaning and role of their content, not merely its appearance. Elements such as nav, main, article, button, and heading elements give browsers and assistive technology useful structure and native behaviour. They improve accessibility, maintainability, and document understanding, while CSS remains responsible for presentation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands semantics as meaning and native behaviour, not a list of HTML5 tags.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Replacing native controls with styled div elements or choosing elements from their default appearance.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the limits of ARIA and when a neutral div is appropriate.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Semantic elements communicate what content is or does.
Native elements often include keyboard and accessibility behaviour.
Document landmarks and headings make navigation easier.
Choose an element by meaning, then style it with CSS.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Semantic HTML uses elements whose names and built-in roles describe the purpose of their content. A nav identifies a major group of navigation links, main identifies the document's dominant content, and article represents a self-contained composition.

Semantics matter because different users and tools consume the same document. Screen readers can navigate landmarks and headings, search engines can better understand structure, and developers can recognise intent without reverse-engineering classes such as blue-box or clickable-text.

Native interactive elements also provide behaviour. A button is focusable, activates from expected keyboard keys, participates in forms, and exposes a button role. A div with a click handler provides none of that automatically.

For example, a page can use header, nav, main, article, and footer while CSS gives them any visual arrangement. The semantics remain useful even when styles fail to load or the content is read by a non-visual tool.

The boundary is that semantic markup is not a promise of good design by itself. Elements must be chosen correctly, headings need a logical hierarchy, images need appropriate alternatives, and CSS still controls appearance. When no meaningful native element fits, a div or span is the correct neutral container. Semantic structure also makes progressive enhancement more dependable. Links still navigate and forms still submit before optional JavaScript loads, so the document retains a working baseline instead of depending on a custom widget for every task.

sections.title: Meaning survives presentation
sections.content: HTML describes the content model; CSS describes its presentation. Semantic choices let a browser expose structure and behaviour without depending on a visual layout. This is especially important for controls, headings, lists, tables, forms, and page landmarks.

sections.title: Prefer native semantics before adding roles
sections.content: ARIA can supplement semantics when a native element cannot express a custom widget, but it does not automatically add keyboard interaction or browser behaviour. A native button is therefore safer than role=button on a div. Neutral div and span elements remain valuable when the group has no specific meaning.

sections.title: Meaningful element versus visual imitation
sections.content:
| Need | Semantic HTML | Visual-only imitation |
|---|---|---|
| Page navigation | nav containing links | div class=navigation |
| Action | button | clickable div |
| Ordered steps | ol with li | numbered paragraphs |
| Main page content | main | div class=main |

sections.title: Structure a small article page
sections.content:
```html
Field Notes
Topics

How bees navigate

Bees combine several environmental signals.

Published by Field Notes
``` The source communicates page regions, content hierarchy, and an action even before any CSS is applied.

questions.question: What is the difference between main, article, section, and div?
questions.title: main, article, section, and div compared
questions.direct_answer: main wraps the page's dominant unique content, article wraps a self-contained composition that can stand on its own, section groups a thematic part of a document and normally has a heading, and div is a neutral container with no added meaning. Choose the most specific correct element; use div when the grouping exists only for styling or scripting.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses structural elements from content meaning.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using section as a styled div or putting repeated site chrome inside main.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that visual card design and semantic element choice are independent.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: main identifies the dominant content of the page.
article should make sense as an independent composition.
section groups a thematic part and usually needs a heading.
div is correct when no semantic element matches.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
main identifies the dominant content of the document body. A page normally exposes one non-hidden main landmark, excluding repeated site navigation, logos, and footers. Its job is page-level, not simply a class name for a large container.

article represents a self-contained composition that could be reused or distributed independently, such as a news story, forum post, product review, or comment. An article may contain sections when its own content has themes.

section groups a thematic part of a document when no more specific element fits. It normally has a heading that names that theme. A section is not a generic wrapper used only to create padding.

div carries no additional meaning. For example, a div can group an icon and label for a styling hook, while a product review containing its own heading and author is better represented as an article.

These elements can be nested when the content model supports it, but more semantics are not automatically better. The boundary is honest meaning: if a group has no standalone purpose, theme, or landmark role, a div is clearer than inventing one.

sections.title: Ask how independently the content makes sense
sections.content: main answers which content dominates this page. article answers whether the composition can stand alone. section answers whether the content forms a named theme. div makes no claim beyond grouping.

sections.title: Semantics come from content, not box shape
sections.content: The same visual card could be an article, section, list item, or div depending on what it contains and how it participates in the document. Reusable visual styles should therefore be attached through classes rather than assuming every card has the same semantic element.

sections.title: Element choice
sections.content:
Dominant unique page content? -> main
Self-contained composition?    -> article
Named thematic grouping?       -> section
Only styling/script grouping?  -> div

sections.title: Nest elements according to their content role
sections.content:
```html

City guide

Food

Market review

Fresh produce every morning.

``` The page has one dominant main, Food is a named theme, the review stands alone, and the decorative hook is neutral.

questions.question: How should heading levels be structured on an HTML page?
questions.title: Logical HTML heading hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: Heading levels should represent the document hierarchy: h1 names the page, h2 starts a major section, h3 starts a subsection of that h2, and so on. Do not choose levels for font size or skip levels merely for appearance. A single clear h1 is the safest convention, and CSS should control how every level looks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner separates content hierarchy from typography.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Picking a heading tag for its default size or using nested h1 elements as an automatic reset.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention component context and the absence of a dependable automatic outline algorithm.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use heading levels to describe nesting, not visual size.
A page should normally have one clear h1.
Move to h3 when the content is a subsection of an h2.
Style headings with CSS instead of selecting a false level.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Headings create a navigable outline of the content. h1 is the highest level and normally names the page, h2 identifies major sections under it, and h3 identifies subsections within an h2.

The level comes from structure, not visual design. If a heading should look small, I keep the correct level and style it with a class. Choosing h4 because its browser default is smaller gives assistive technology a misleading hierarchy.

For example, a recipe page can use h1 for the recipe name, h2 for Ingredients and Method, and h3 for separate method stages. Moving directly from that h1 to an h3 would imply a missing level unless the surrounding structure already establishes the h2.

A single h1 is the clearest cross-browser and accessibility convention for a page. Current HTML does not create an automatic heading outline that safely resets nested h1 elements, so each heading should have an explicit, logical level.

The boundary is reusable components: a card component may appear under different ancestors. It can receive its heading level from context or expose content without pretending it always owns one fixed document level.

sections.title: Headings are a table of contents
sections.content: Read only the headings in order. They should summarize the page and show which ideas belong under which parent idea. If the sequence sounds like a useful table of contents, the hierarchy is probably doing its job.

sections.title: Visual size and semantic rank are independent
sections.content: CSS can make an h2 quieter than body text or an h3 visually prominent without changing the document hierarchy. Screen-reader heading navigation uses the semantic levels, not the font size. This separation lets responsive design change typography while the outline stays stable.

sections.title: A logical recipe outline
sections.content:
h1 Vegetable soup
  h2 Ingredients
  h2 Method
    h3 Prepare vegetables
    h3 Simmer
  h2 Storage

sections.title: Keep levels aligned with content nesting
sections.content:
```html

Vegetable soup

Ingredients

  • Carrots

Method

Prepare vegetables

Wash and chop them.

Simmer

Cook until tender.

``` The markup remains a useful outline even if CSS gives every heading a custom size.

questions.question: What is the difference between strong, em, b, and i in HTML?
questions.title: strong, em, b, and i semantics
questions.direct_answer: strong marks strong importance, seriousness, or urgency; em marks stress emphasis that can change a sentence's meaning; b draws attention without adding importance; and i marks text set apart in an alternate voice or conventional category. Their default bold or italic styles are incidental—use CSS when the requirement is only visual.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner chooses text-level elements by meaning rather than browser defaults.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming b and i are deprecated or using strong for every visually bold label.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how moving stress emphasis can change a sentence's interpretation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: strong communicates importance or urgency.
em communicates stress emphasis in the sentence.
b draws attention without extra importance.
i marks an alternate voice, term, or conventional category.
Use CSS for decoration with no semantic meaning.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
strong and em add meaning. strong marks content with strong importance, seriousness, or urgency, such as a safety warning. em adds stress emphasis, similar to changing which word is stressed when speaking a sentence.

b and i also have defined uses, but they do not mean generic bold and italic. b can draw attention to a keyword without increasing its importance. i can mark an alternate voice, technical term, taxonomic name, or another conventionally offset phrase.

For example, “Do not share your password” can wrap the prohibition in strong because it is important. In “I asked for the blue version,” em around blue communicates spoken contrast. A product name highlighted only for brand styling needs a span and CSS instead.

Browsers commonly render strong and b as bold and em and i as italic, but appearance is not the deciding rule. Styles can be changed completely while their meaning remains.

The boundary is author intent. If there is no importance, stress, attention convention, or alternate voice to communicate, a semantic text element would invent meaning. CSS font-weight or font-style on a neutral span is then the honest choice.

sections.title: Meaning first, default style second
sections.content: Two pairs may look alike in an unstyled browser, but their semantics differ. Read the sentence aloud and ask whether importance, spoken stress, attention, or alternate voice is actually present before choosing the element.

sections.title: Stress can change interpretation
sections.content: Moving em between words can change the implied correction: “I asked for blue” differs depending on whether I, asked, or blue receives stress. strong raises importance without representing that vocal shift. b and i are useful when publishing conventions require attention or alternate voice but not those stronger meanings.

sections.title: Choose by intended meaning
sections.content:
| Element | Meaning | Not simply |
|---|---|---|
| strong | Strong importance or urgency | Bold text |
| em | Stress emphasis | Italic text |
| b | Attention without extra importance | Any bold style |
| i | Alternate voice or conventional category | Any italic style |

sections.title: Markup meaning and styling separately
sections.content:
```html

Warning: Disconnect power before opening the case.

I asked for the blue cable, not the black one.

Search for the keyword accessibility.

The phrase carpe diem is Latin.

Northwind is styled only for branding.

``` Each semantic element has a reason that still makes sense if its default bold or italic styling is removed.

questions.question: How do HTML landmarks improve keyboard and screen-reader navigation?
questions.title: HTML landmarks and page navigation
questions.direct_answer: Landmark elements such as header, nav, main, aside, and footer divide a page into recognisable regions that screen-reader users can jump between. A skip link lets keyboard users bypass repeated navigation and reach main content. Landmarks must be used for real regions, and repeated landmarks such as multiple nav elements need accessible labels.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can connect native landmarks to practical assistive navigation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating many unnamed landmarks or assuming CSS visual order changes focus order.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Combine landmarks, skip links, headings, and logical DOM order as one navigation system.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Landmarks expose major page regions for assistive navigation.
A skip link moves keyboard focus past repeated content.
Use one clear main landmark for dominant page content.
Give multiple landmarks of the same type distinct accessible labels.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
HTML landmark elements expose the major regions of a page through the accessibility tree. A screen-reader user can move directly among navigation, main content, complementary content, and footer regions instead of reading every element in source order.

Keyboard users benefit from a skip link at the beginning of the page. Its target is the main content, so someone tabbing through repeated site links can bypass them and begin the page-specific task quickly.

For example, a documentation page can have nav aria-label='Primary' for site sections and another nav aria-label='On this page' for heading links. The distinct labels let a landmark list explain which navigation is which.

Landmarks should identify large meaningful regions, not wrap every card or paragraph. Too many unnamed landmarks create another long list to search. A page normally exposes one visible main region, while header and footer become landmarks according to their context.

Visual reordering does not change the keyboard sequence. The source order should remain logical, focus indicators must stay visible, and a skip target may need tabindex=-1 in some focus-management patterns. Landmarks improve navigation, but they do not repair an illogical DOM. The accessible name of a landmark should describe its purpose, such as Primary or Course topics, rather than repeat its role. A landmark list then stays short, distinct, and useful.

sections.title: A map plus a shortcut
sections.content: Landmarks provide the map of major regions. A skip link provides a direct shortcut to the page's main task. Headings then provide detailed navigation within that region. These layers work together without requiring a custom keyboard widget.

sections.title: Useful landmarks need names and restraint
sections.content: A native nav element already exposes navigation semantics. When several nav regions exist, aria-label or aria-labelledby gives each a distinct name. Labels should not repeat the word navigation unnecessarily because the role is already announced. Generic regions only become landmarks when they receive an accessible name, so a labelled section should still represent a meaningful region.

sections.title: Two navigation paths through the same page
sections.content:
Keyboard: first Tab -> Skip to main content -> main heading
Screen reader: landmark list -> Primary / Main / On this page / Footer
Within main: heading list -> chosen lesson section

sections.title: Provide distinct navigation landmarks and a skip link
sections.content:
```html Skip to main content
Topics

CSS layout guide

Grid

Grid

Shared tracks align content.

Help and policies
``` The two nav regions have distinct names, and the first keyboard link bypasses repeated site navigation.
